title: [Launch] D.R.I.F.T. My First Solo Game Is Now Live and AI Tools Made It Possible
author: BlueStyrk
selftext:
Hey everyone!  
I just wanted to stop by and share something huge (for me, at least): **my first game, D.R.I.F.T., is officially released on Steam today.**

  
 [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4036980/DRIFT/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4036980/DRIFT/)

Some of you might remember my earlier posts here, your feedback, insights, encouragement and even criticism had a real impact on the project, so thank you.

I built *D.R.I.F.T.* as a **solo dev**, and I can say with absolute certainty that **AI tools didn’t replace the work, they** ***enabled*** **it**. With limited resources and abilities, no team, and a full development pipeline to handle alone, AI became a kind of *force multiplier*:

* It **cut my production time nearly in half**.
* It helped me stay focused instead of drowning in endless tasks.
* It let me iterate faster, unblock ideas, and solve problems I would’ve spent days on before.
* It supported me in writing, coding assistance, narrative design, and polishing the overall experience.

But, and this is important: **AI didn’t build the game for me**.  
Every system, design choice, mission, script, bug fix, and piece of content still required *a lot* of human effort, testing, rewriting, balancing, and stubbornness. AI tools didn’t replace the work; they amplified what I could achieve alone.

For me, the biggest win is that **AI helped a single developer from Uruguay turn a long-time dream into a finished, published game**. That’s something I never thought I’d be able to say.

If you're curious about how AI-assisted solo dev can reach the finish line, or if you just like space exploration sims, feel free to check out the game or try the demo.

Thanks again to this community, genuinely. Your discussions and advice helped me push through and make this a reality.

comments.author: umen
comments.body: Can you elaborate on how exactly it helped and what was your pipeline, and congratulations on your release!

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
Thank you! I really appreciate it. And yes, releasing D.R.I.F.T. has been quite the journey and a huge achievement.

As for how AI fit into my workflow: I used it mostly as a *development companion*, not as a replacement for actual production work. Since I was building the game solo, AI helped me think through architecture, unblock design issues, and draft the initial structure of certain systems. It gave me a way to iterate faster, especially in the early stages, but every mechanic and feature still required a lot of hands-on coding, testing, rewriting, and fine-tuning on my part.

For visuals and planning, it also helped where I didn’t have the resources of a full team. Think of it as a kind of “virtual support crew” that sped up the process, not something that takes over the creative or technical decisions.

I prefer not to share every detail of my pipeline, but the essence is:  
**AI amplified my work, it didn’t drive it.** The game only exists because of a year of consistent effort, problem-solving, and iteration.

Thanks again for the kind words and if you give the game or the demo a try, I hope you enjoy it!

replies.author: umen
replies.body: Oh, I see. Well, this is the same for all of the developers. I, for example, use only VS Code and Codex, and yes, there's a 30% improvement in speed, maybe more. But you need to be the gatekeeper, the supervisor of the output code. What about graphics?

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
Thanks again! And yes, I completely agree. As useful as an LLM is, you always need to be in control. Not only to be aware of what you're generating, but also to oversee the code, the architecture, and every suggestion it offers. It speeds things up, but it's not a complete or flawless solution. There's no perfect answer; it's always a creative process.

I think there's a lot of confusion when someone says, "I used AI to create a game." Many people, I think, imagine that you simply type "make me a game" and it magically appears. When the reality is very different: it's still a long and complex process where the human element is constantly the creative engine, reviewing, correcting, redesigning, and making everything work.

Regarding the graphics: I mainly used AI to generate base images, which I then modified myself (with my limited design skills, which is noticeable). It was a practical decision: I'm a soloDev working by myself the entire project, with a very limited budget and questionable artistic ability, so using AI for concept art and base images saved me a lot of time and money. But, I insist, it didn't replace the work; it simply gave me something to build upon.

I also used it to generate promotional material.

For me, AI is a tool that helps developers move faster, not something that replaces them.

Again, thank you very much for your comments; they raise a discussion that I think is very healthy to have.

replies.author: umen
replies.body: I'm only a solo developer, so I can relate. I'm in the process and looking to find time-saving processes. AI is a big player here. Can you share what you're using for image creation and AI code?

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
I totally understand. As a solo developer, anything that saves time and mental health without sacrificing quality is greatly appreciated.

For visuals, I've primarily used [Leonardo.AI](http://Leonardo.AI) to generate basic concepts, which I then refine and edit myself (my design skills are… let's just say "functional" 😅). It's also been very helpful for creating promotional materials and short videos.

For coding assistance and iteration, I mainly rely on ChatGPT, as it's where I've established the most robust workflow. I experimented with Gemini, but I haven't yet found a workflow that feels smooth or reliable enough. That doesn't mean it isn't a very good tool; it produces some interesting results, but it's taken me a while to adapt it to my workflow

For audio, especially promotional materials, trailers, and short stories narrated by the game's AI, I've been using ElevenLabs. If you're curious, I'm uploading the short stories and promotional content here: [https://www.youtube.com/@resilientLogic](https://www.youtube.com/@resilientLogic)

As you can see there is nothing sophisticated or expensive: all the tools are free, and the rest is mostly about defining clear objectives, reviewing, iterating, and judging whether the solution truly requires AI. Sometimes AI is not the right solution to every problem.

As you said, AI is a key factor, but it's the workflow that really makes the difference and without a creative mind in the background to generate ideas, identify and define challenges, and monitor results.

I hope this helps you create your own workflow system.

replies.author: umen
replies.body: Do you use Codex? I found it very good, and I'm considering buying a Cursor license now, which I use at work and it's like magic for developers

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
I actually don’t use Codex. I’ve been seriously considering getting a paid plan to improve my basic toolkit, but since this is my first project the budget has been… well, close to zero.  
Now that things are moving forward, I’m hoping to upgrade the tools I use.

It’s definitely a process figuring out what works, what doesn’t, and which tools fit best with each person’s workflow.  
Thanks for the recommendation!

replies.author: gardenia856
replies.body: The trick with AI graphics is to lock a style early and build a repeatable pipeline. For 2D, SDXL or ComfyUI + ControlNet/IP-Adapter with a small LoRA trained on 30–50 curated refs keeps ships, UI, and decals consistent; fix a seed per asset class, then batch in ComfyUI, clean in Photoshop, and vectorize icons in Figma/Inkscape. Use Tile Diffusion for seamless textures, make PBR maps in Materialize or Substance Sampler, upscale with Topaz/ESRGAN, and pack sprites with TexturePacker. For 3D, block in Blender, auto-rig in Mixamo, and generate trim sheets or decals with SD; it’s fast for LODs and background props. Performance: compress to KTX2/Basis, enforce a shared palette, and set engine import presets for mips and max sizes. For promo, I rough in SD/Midjourney, then do typography and layout in Figma. I’ve used Supabase for auth and PlayFab for telemetry; when I needed quick REST on a crusty SQL DB, DreamFactory generated endpoints so I could wire up build analytics fast. Keep a fixed pipeline and style guide so everything feels like one game.

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
Wow, this is incredibly detailed! Thank you for taking the time to break down the whole workflow. It basically reads like a mini–best-practice guide for building a consistent AI-assisted art pipeline, and there are several parts I hadn’t considered integrating into my current process.

Right now I’m fully focused on getting through the first wave of fixes and updates after release, but once that settles, I’m definitely going to revisit this and see what I can apply to improve visual consistency and production efficiency. Things like locking style early, using fixed seeds, and building a repeatable pipeline make a lot of sense for scaling up the art without losing cohesion.

Really appreciate you sharing this, it’s the kind of info that can genuinely help push the project to the next level.

replies.author: BlueStyrk

Thank you so much! I really appreciate it and I’m especially grateful for the advice you gave me earlier about improving the Steam page. Those adjustments genuinely helped boost the wishlist numbers, so you definitely had a hand in that success.

So far, I’ve managed to accomplish all the goals I set for this release: the game is published, the reception has been positive, the production costs are covered, and little by little a solid foundation is forming for new projects and challenges ahead.

Thanks again for the support and for taking the time to help it really means a lot!

I’m really glad to hear you’re working on a new game and already aiming for a 2026 release, that’s fantastic news. Let’s make sure it gets the visibility it deserves.

Thanks again for the support; it’s genuinely revitalizing.

comments.author: rage997
comments.body:
it reminds me of dark orbit. Has there been some inspiration? 

Also, those galactic gates remind me of the stargate. Some inspiration here too?

Looks great btw nice work!

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
Thanks a lot! Really appreciate the comment and the support.  
I’m glad you liked it.

Being honest, I didn’t know *DarkOrbit.* To be honest, I haven’t played much videogames overall, so there wasn’t any direct inspiration from there. My main inspiration (even if it’s not as obvious now) was **NAEV**. It was the starting point, though the project eventually evolved into something quite different.

As for the jumpgates: absolutely, they’re a clear nod to **Stargate**. I’ve been a big fan of the series for years, so that was my little homage.

And of course, the whole sci-fi/space vibe comes from a lifetime of reading Asimov, Clarke, Herbert… all those giants that shaped my imagination.

Thanks again for the kind words!

replies.author: rage997
replies.body:
Seems like we have many interests in common OP!

I have pretty much read everything Asimov has ever wrote and I am a huge (seriously, huge) fan of stargate. In that matter, are you aware of the fact that a new stargate show is coming? It's official now and it's going to be a amazon show

replies.author: BlueStyrk
replies.body:
Same here, I’ve always been an avid reader, and those stories pretty much shaped and illuminated my teenage years. Now, with a few more decades on my back, I still try to hold onto that sense of imagination and the dream that one day humanity might actually wander through the stars the way those characters did.

And yes, I heard about the new Stargate show, and I’m genuinely excited… but I’ll admit I’m also a bit nervous. A lot of great franchises have come back only to be turned into purely commercial products, losing the essence that made them special. I really hope this revival goes more the way of Dr Who’s comeback years ago (even if I haven’t kept up with the last few seasons).

Fingers crossed, I’d love to see Stargate return with the heart and spirit it deserves.
